accuracy.evidence: Checked against the Year 3 Forces and magnets statutory requirement (compare how things move on different surfaces) and the non-statutory notes (friction as a force between surfaces). Friction is described as a contact force acting along the surfaces and against motion or attempted motion. The roll distances (ice 3.0, wood 1.6, carpet 0.7, sandpaper 0.4 m) and slide angles (about 6°, 20°, 30°, 40°) are labelled in the adult text as a model; their order matches classroom results, and the wood and sandpaper angles fit typical static friction coefficients (tan 20° ≈ 0.36 for wood on wood, tan 40° ≈ 0.84 for a rough abrasive surface).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips at this age: moving objects stop because the push 'runs out' (an impetus idea); friction drawn in the direction of motion; soft carpet thought to let things roll further; friction seen only as a nuisance; and unfair tests that change the push as well as the surface.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfrict models surfaces themselves: four textured floors with a same-push roll test, a block whose friction arrow flips as the learner drags it each way, a fair-test check that compares pushes, a slippery-to-grippy ranking, a tilting ramp with a per-surface slide angle and a walker that slips with smooth soles. flagshove varies push strength and direction and flagfvoc matches force words; neither has surfaces, friction arrows or slide angles. Shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees the same push carry the car 3.0 m on ice but 0.7 m on carpet before being told rough means more friction; drags the block and sees the friction arrow always point back; gets a 'not fair yet' message if the push changes between floors; ranks floors from their own results; and finds that sandpaper must be tilted about twice as steeply as wood before the block slides.

predictions.evidence: Six predictions, each led by a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'carpet, because it is soft', 'friction points the same way', 'just push hard each time', 'wood has more friction because it is hard', 'smooth wood needs the steeper ramp', and 'friction is always a nuisance'.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; wrong answers are tagged soft, same, with, down, fair or runout and each tag has its own message: soft surfaces make more friction, the surface matters, friction never acts with the motion, down is gravity not friction, a fair test changes one thing, and things stop because of friction not because a push runs out.

readability.evidence: Kid text Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.9 (family target ≤ 5): short sentences, the word friction defined in the first sentence, concrete examples (toy car, carpet, ice, shoes, bike brakes). Adult text grade 8.6 (target ≤ 10) names the Year 3 requirement and five common mistakes.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases. Each kid paragraph does one job: define friction and its direction, rough versus smooth, the fair test, friction being useful. Adult paragraphs give curriculum placement, the physics and the model caveat, the mistakes list and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in both themes: the track, 0-4 m scale, results bars, ranking cards and ramp fit the 390 px canvas; the ramp angle and 'It slides!' labels were moved to the empty upper left so they no longer collide with the drag handle; floor and push buttons wrap to two rows without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: floor choice with aria-pressed, Gentle/Strong push, Push the car, Pull right/left, the four ranking buttons, Tilt up/Lower 5°, sole choice and Take a step. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with the distance, arrow direction or angle. walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA was clean in both themes on desktop and phone.
